Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-14 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Samira Patel (Redwood SE), Ethan Cole (Perf Eng), Maya Lin (Redwood Solutions); Tom Nguyen (EdgeScale), Priya Menon (EdgeScale), Luis Rodriguez (EdgeScale), Aisha Karim (EdgeScale SRE)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): ok everyone can hear me? testing 1 2
[00:05] Tom Nguyen: yes loud and clear, thanks for setting this up. we've got Priya and Aisha on the line too.
[00:10] Jordan: great. objective for today: go deep on rope scaling and moE routing costs across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen, and map that to Redwood Dedicated / Private options. we'll try to capture concrete configs you can run.
[00:25] Priya: yeah, for context we run a mix of chat assistants and retrieval-augmented Q&A. latency SLOs are 120ms p50 and 400ms p99 in EU region, cost sensitivity is high. most of our traffic is short prompts but we have occasional long completion tails.
[00:40] Samira (SE): good, that helps. can you confirm current stack? are you on k8s + Triton or self-hosted containers?
[00:50] Aisha: currently k8s on-prem for most requests, but we front some traffic through a cloud edge layer. we use Triton for some model endpoints and a homegrown sharding for embeddings.
[01:05] Ethan (Perf Eng): quick note: Triton has different attention kernel behavior for rope vs rotary; that can cause variance. Redwood runtime picks kernels per model but we need the prompt length distribution to tune.
[01:25] Luis (CTO): we also evaluate MoE for some routing-heavy tasks; curious about the cost overhead and how kv-caching interacts with MoE experts.
[01:35] Samira: yup, MoE routing adds two main costs: routing compute (sparse dispatch) and increased activation memory during expert execution. if you have many small requests, the routing overhead can dominate unless you batch across requests or use a routing threshold.
[01:55] Tom: can you expand on routing threshold? we saw documentation mentioning top-k gating, but not sure how that translates to prod.
[02:05] Samira: sure — in many MoE implementations there's a top-k gate per token — often top-1 or top-2. if you bias towards top-1 you reduce cross-expert scatter but might worsen load balance; top-2 gives better balance but more memory/compute. Redwood supports routing policies that can map top-k to cost tiers; eg top-1 fallback to smaller expert set for latency sensitive routes.
[02:30] Priya: how does rope scaling affect this? we've seen hallucinations when running Qwen with longer contexts — suspect rope misalignment?
[02:40] Ethan: good question. RoPE decay and scaling frequency (the alpha/beta params in some libs) change relative position encodings at long sequences. Qwen and some Mistral variants use different RoPE implementations — that affects KV cache re-use across requests. if you reuse KV cache when sequence lengths vary a lot you can get phase misalignment.
[03:05] Jordan: so is the recommendation to normalize sequence length distribution or to rebase caches per conversation?
[03:12] Samira: generally rebase per conversation window. for short-chat workloads we keep KV caches small and evict aggressively. for long context RAG sessions we maintain per-session KV and use anchored rebase at known keyframe tokens to avoid phase drift.
[03:30] Tom: you said phase drift — can that explain the quality drop with our Llama-2-13B runs after 1k tokens?
[03:38] Ethan: yes, could be. also check if you're using 4-bit quant with group size mismatch — quantization can amplify small position encoding errors because precision is lower in attention scores.
[03:55] Priya: we've mostly been testing q4_k_m and make heavy use of rotary. the outputs degrade at 900-1200 tokens, which lines up. any mitigations short of staying full-precision?
[04:10] Samira: a few levers: 1) use per-layer quantization calibration and run a small eval set to catch regressions, 2) increase KV eviction frequency and re-synchronize rope anchors, 3) for MoE flows, prefer top-1 gating for latency-sensitive paths and reserve top-2 for batch offline processing.
[04:35] Luis: ok about batching — we balance throughput and tail latency. what batching policies does Redwood recommend for small prompt workloads with occasional long tails?
[04:45] Maya (Solutions): Redwood Optimize has a suggestion engine — for that pattern we often use adaptive batching: small fixed micro-batches at the edge to satisfy p50, plus opportunistic aggregation in a 5–10ms window to improve GPU throughput for p95. but you must cap batch size to avoid p99 blowups on long-context requests.
[05:10] Tom: what's the recommended max batch for Llama-2-13B on A10G or A100?
[05:17] Ethan: approximate numbers: A100 80GB with q4_gemu you can do batch 8 at 4k tokens comfortably for throughput; A10G closer to batch 4 at 2k tokens. these are very workload dependent — your token distribution matters. we'll produce a table after seeing your traces.
[05:35] Priya: can Redwood Dedicated run both MoE and dense models in same pool with smart routing? we want to avoid cold transfers.
[05:45] Samira: yes, smart routing can pin requests by policy. we can keep small dense fallback instances and route to MoE when capacity and latency allow. routing policies can also prefer local experts in Private deployments to reduce cross-host traffic.
[06:05] Aisha: on on-prem VPC/KMS: if we adopt Redwood Private on our network, how does KMS key rotation and audit logging integrate? we need HSM-backed keys for compliance.
[06:15] Jordan: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we stream audit logs to your SIEM and include cryptographic attestations. Maya can follow up with architecture doc.
[06:30] Maya: will do. I'll schedule a KMS deep-dive.
[06:35] Tom: great. back to KV cache — what's the typical hit-rate improvements you see with conversational workloads?
[06:42] Samira: for stable dialog flows we often see KV hit rates 40–70% depending on session affinity. for stateless short prompts it's lower. hit-rate is very sensitive to session sharding and rekey frequency.
[07:00] Jordan: can you describe an experiment we should run in the trial to surface these effects?
[07:05] Samira: recommended: replay a 2-hour production-like trace with the exact prompt distribution. run three configs: dense full-precision, dense q4, and MoE (top-1) q4. measure p50/p95/p99, token cost, and KV hit-rate. include a stress test where 10% of requests are long-tail >2k tokens.
[07:35] Priya: how do we instrument the traces? can Redwood ingest our trace format?
[07:40] Ethan: we can accept jaeger traces and token-level traces in the shared bench schema. Samira will upload the microbench harness that wraps your trace.
[07:50] Tom: earlier you mentioned rope anchors; does that mean we need to modify model code or is it runtime-level?
[07:58] Samira: mostly runtime-level. Redwood can apply anchor rebasing at the KV layer. however if you changed the model's RoPE implementation (e.g. different scaling constants), you may need a tiny shim. we have prebuilt shims for common forks of Llama, Mistral, and Qwen.
[08:20] Luis: any gotchas with Qwen? we saw better perplexity but weird tail latency spikes.
[08:28] Ethan: Qwen's attention chunking and RoPE implementation can cause uneven kernel loads — some sequence lengths map to kernels that are much heavier. That explains latency spikes at certain prompt lengths. Redwood runtime maps kernels to hardware and will try to smooth by re-chunking when latencies spike.
[08:50] Aisha: for Private deployments, if we host on-prem how does autoscaling work? we can't just spin GPUs on demand.
[08:58] Maya: for Private you define capacity tiers and burst policies. we use warm pools and pre-warmed containers; autoscaling is capacity-based rather than ephemeral. you can set strict capacity caps to match hardware procurement.
[09:15] Tom: cost question — MoE looked cheaper per token in papers, but in practice routing overhead looks expensive. what's the delta we should expect?
[09:25] Samira: on average, MoE reduces param cost but increases routing and memory overhead. For mixed short-request workloads MoE can be 10–40% more expensive unless you aggregate requests to amortize routing. For very large batch offline workloads MoE shines — cost per useful token can be lower.
[09:45] Priya: are there Redwood-console metrics we can use to monitor MoE health?
[09:50] Jordan: yes, we emit routing distribution, expert load imbalance, routing latency, per-expert mem pressure, and KV hit-rate. you can set alerts on imbalance and per-expert OOM risk.
[10:05] Tom: ok can we pivot to a concrete sensitivity test: change rope scaling parameter by 10% and run q4 quant — what effect do we expect on quality?
[10:15] Ethan: small changes in RoPE scaling can reduce alignment at long distances; with q4 you can see BLEU/ROUGE style drops or task-specific metric regressions of 2–8% on long-context tests. that's why calibration is critical.
[10:30] Priya: do you recommend post-training quantization or PTQ+small calibration dataset?
[10:36] Samira: PTQ with per-layer calibration is the sweet spot. LLM INT8 can be finicky; we usually recommend q4 with per-channel scale for minimal regressions. we'll share recommended calibration sets.
[10:50] Jordan: quick run-of-show for the trial: Redwood will provision a Dedicated trial with a single A100 pool, install runtime with your two Llama/Mistral/Qwen images, run the three configs Samira suggested, and deliver a report with traces and kernel-level breakdown.
[11:10] Tom: timeline? we need results in two weeks ideally.
[11:15] Jordan: doable — we'll need your trace and sample prompts within 48 hours.
[11:22] Tom: ok we'll push that today.
[11:25] Priya: one more question on quant and on-prem HSM: does encryption at rest impact runtime performance meaningfully?
[11:33] Maya: key ops (decrypting model keys) are one-time at start; per-request encryption isn't typical. however when using HSM for per-request signing or attestation you can add ~1–2ms per request depending on your HSM latency. good to benchmark.
[11:50] Aisha: noted. for SLA we'll need to budget that.
[12:00] Samira: also watch out for network fanout when MoE covers experts across hosts; cross-host IO can kill latency. pin experts or use replication to reduce remote calls.
[12:18] Luis: replication increases memory cost but helps p99. fine tradeoff.
[12:25] Jordan: ok let's surface some concrete configs now — Samira do you want to share recommended batch/quant/rope defaults per model?
[12:32] Samira: yes — high level, for Llama-2-13B dense: q4_gemu, batch 4 on A10, batch 8 on A100; KV eviction after 512 tokens for mixed workloads; rope anchor every 256 tokens for long sessions. For Mistral-large: q4_0 with per-layer calib, batch 6 on A100; Qwen-7B: prefer q4_k with smaller group size, batch 10 on A100 but watch for kernel spikes, set a fallback per-request single-expert path for p99. MoE configurations: top-1 for latency, top-2 for batch throughput, and always test with and without routing cache.
[13:25] Priya: can you spell out 'rope anchor every 256' — is that a token count or wall time?
[13:30] Samira: token count. we rebase at natural conversation checkpoints (end of turns) and every N tokens for long-running sessions. choose a power-of-two close to your median session length.
[13:45] Tom: perfect. anything else on observability?
[13:50] Ethan: collect kernel-level counters and routing histograms; we'll provide a dashboard template.
[13:58] Jordan: looks like we're near the top of hour. recap of next steps then?
[14:03] Tom: we'll upload traces and prompt distribution today.
[14:06] Jordan: Jordan will send trial invite and pricing. Samira will upload microbench harness and kv scripts. Maya will share KMS/doc follow-up. schedule follow-up in two weeks.
